title: Lattice Deduction Transformers
claim: Combining lattice-based deduction with search in a recurrent transformer reaches far higher accuracy than prior reasoners at much lower compute.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; lattice diagram plus architecture, then scatter plot
description: Panel (a) is a method diagram. On the left is a Hasse diagram of the subset lattice over {1,2,3,4}, from the full set 1234 at the top down to the empty set at the bottom. A red arrow runs from node 234 (x) down to node 3 (x'), showing a deduction step. In the centre is a vertical block diagram: a Lattice encoding x box feeds a dashed 4× transformer block (LayerNorm, Multi-Head Attention, LayerNorm, Feed Forward in pastel colours), then a Lattice encoding x' box. A 16× loop returns through a red Branch box. Panel (b) is a log-x scatter plot of Sudoku-Extreme accuracy against training plus solving compute in PFLOPs. Red LDT points sit far up and to the left of grey square baselines (EqR, Sotaku v2, TRM, HRM). Dashed lines mark the LDT portfolio of 5 variants at the top.
caption: (a) The Lattice Deduction Transformer (LDT) performs deduction on a lattice using a recurrent transformer which is alternated with search via stochastic branching. (b) Sudoku-Extreme accuracy against the estimated FLOPs of training plus solving the 422,786-puzzle test set.
abstract: We introduce the Lattice Deduction Transformer (LDT), a recurrent transformer that approximates logically sound deduction by projecting its latent state through a lattice between forward passes. We train on-policy in a process that mirrors deduction in a search-based constraint solver and supervise training via a domain-agnostic approximation of the set of solution candidates based on abstract interpretation. An $800$K-parameter LDT outperforms prior small recurrent reasoners on Sudoku-Extreme with under $2\%$ of their estimated training FLOPs, solving $99.999\%$ of the $422{,}786$ test puzzles. The model is nearly always sound, in that it gives a wrong answer for $4$ of $1.27$M puzzle evaluations, and otherwise returns a correct answer or abstains. A $1.8$M-parameter LDT variant reaches $99.8\%$ accuracy on Maze-Hard. Our code is available at github.com/lcrh/lattice-deduction-transformers.
